record.question:
A company must connect its on-premises headquarters privately to VPCs in several US Regions. The VPC CIDRs do not overlap. Traffic must use dedicated connectivity, remain available after a Direct Connect location fails, and avoid a separate physical connection for every Region. The requirement is headquarters-to-VPC access, not transit between VPCs.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a LAG with two Direct Connect connections at one location. Connect private VIFs to a Direct Connect gateway and associate a virtual private gateway from each VPC.
Connect a Transit Gateway in each Region to headquarters through redundant internet-based Site-to-Site VPN tunnels, and configure routes for the VPCs.

Use redundant customer devices and Direct Connect connections at two diverse locations. Connect private VIFs to a Direct Connect gateway, associate each VPC's virtual private gateway, and configure redundant BGP routes.
Connect redundant Direct Connect circuits directly to one VPC. Peer that VPC with the other regional VPCs and route their headquarters traffic through the peered VPC's connection.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. A Direct Connect gateway can associate virtual private gateways in multiple Regions, avoiding a physical circuit per Region. Private VIFs provide the relevant VPC connectivity. Diverse physical locations and customer devices remove the single-location failure present in a one-location design, provided routing and capacity support failover.

<<1>> aggregates connections but leaves a shared location dependency. Multiple links in one LAG do not satisfy the stated location-failure requirement.

<<2>> provides a valid managed network pattern, but its internet-based VPN paths do not meet the dedicated-connectivity constraint.

<<4>> assumes unsupported edge-to-edge routing. A peered VPC cannot use its peer's Direct Connect connection to reach the corporate network.

Separate logical reachability from physical resilience. A Direct Connect gateway is global and supports the multi-Region associations, but does not make a single physical circuit redundant or establish an automatic VPC transit mesh. A Transit Gateway association would use a transit VIF, rather than this private-VIF-to-VGW design.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Direct Connect gateways](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/direct-connect-gateways-intro.html); [Direct Connect redundancy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/toolkit-classic.html); [VPC peering routing limits](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics.html).

diagram_alt: Two diverse Direct Connect locations protect the physical connection while one logical gateway associates VPCs across Regions.

sources.supports: Private VIFs and VGW associations connect on-premises networks to VPCs in multiple Regions, while TGW associations use transit VIFs.
Redundant connections or a VPN backup require appropriate routing and failover, and diverse Direct Connect locations provide stronger physical resilience.
Peering cannot transit a peer VPC to use that peer's Direct Connect connection to an on-premises network.

editorial_notes: Preserved answer 3. Added the physical diversity required by the availability constraint, removed an implied full-mesh transit guarantee, and changed the LAG distractor to a valid configuration that fails location resilience.
